2	Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
3	We evaluate five confidence signals (four instance-level, one per-sample log-probability [LP]) for quality estimation and sample selection on four NER benchmarks using 4B\textendash 8B models.
4	All signals achieve reliable quality estimation, supporting selective prediction.
5	For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD when two conditions are jointly met in our data: low instance degeneracy and adequate LP-quality alignment.

7	Two mechanisms explain this gap: \textit{instance degeneracy} (14\textendash 59\% of instances yield identical F1 scores across all samples) eliminates headroom; \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} prevents exploiting the remainder.
8	Degeneracy is controllable via temperature and training convergence; neither scalar signal combinations nor learned text representations close the gap.
9	Hidden state probes confirm information beyond LP exists in model representations, but the correlation-selection gap persists: richer signals do not improve selection in the high-capability regime.

Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}); entity-token LP shows $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse, indicating compression operates at the representation level, not token aggregation (Appendix~\ref{app:lp_failure_stability}).

\paragraph{Regime boundaries and practical guidelines.}
QE signals collapse at the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17, VC conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}); at the ceiling boundary (CoNLL, degeneracy 59--89\%), LP degrades selection ($-0.85$~pp).
In the moderate regime, LP selection tends to succeed when low degeneracy and adequate alignment are jointly present.
Temperature manipulation provides the primary evidence: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 12.5\% (approaching Few-NERD's 13.8\%), yet LP does not improve selection because alignment remains weak ($\rho{=}0.225$ vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}).
Practitioners should estimate both quantities on a labeled development set; approximate boundaries from our data are degeneracy ${<}$15\% and within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}) \gtrsim 0.3$.
Temperature (40.3\% at $T{=}0.5$ to 12.5\% at $T{=}1.2$) and training convergence (Few-NERD: 14\% at 3 epochs to 31\% at 5; Tables~\ref{tab:fewnerd}, \ref{tab:t_degeneracy}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}) provide controllable levers for degeneracy, though not for alignment.
The SciERC epoch curve corroborates this: at 3 epochs, within-instance alignment is higher ($\rho{=}0.32$ vs.\ $0.28$ at 5 epochs), yet LP selection is worse ($-1.18$ vs.\ $+0.62$~pp; Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}), because lower degeneracy (6.4\%) admits more instances where LP precision is insufficient. Positive correlation is thus necessary but not sufficient for selection.
Calibration methods cannot change selection (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}).

\paragraph{From diagnosis to selection.}
Within-instance LP range serves as a per-instance degeneracy proxy; a degeneracy-aware LP selection strategy (DALS) that gates on this proxy yields modest gains on SciERC and Few-NERD but cannot overcome weak alignment (Appendix~\ref{app:dals}).
Hidden state probes (\S\ref{sec:hidden_probe}) confirm richer information exists in model representations ($+37$\% correlation on SciERC), yet selection degrades (gap closure $-5.1$\% vs.\ LP's $+4.8$\%).
The correlation-selection gap thus extends to model-internal representations, reinforcing the capability-diversity tension.

Five confidence signals achieve reliable quality estimation for LLM-based NER ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC above 0.81), but translating this to sample selection requires both low instance degeneracy and adequate LP-quality alignment (approximate thresholds from our data: ${<}$15\% and $\rho \gtrsim 0.3$).
LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) where both conditions are met; when either is violated, gains fall below detectable thresholds despite 12\textendash 14~pp oracle headroom.

As models improve, degeneracy rises and LP compression intensifies, narrowing the window for test-time selection.

1	\begin{abstract}
2	Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
3	We evaluate five confidence signals (four instance-level, one per-sample log-probability [LP]) for quality estimation and sample selection on four NER benchmarks using 4B\textendash 8B models.
4	All signals achieve reliable quality estimation, supporting selective prediction.
5	For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate LP-quality alignment are present.
6	When either condition is violated, LP gains fall below detectable thresholds despite ${\sim}$13~pp oracle headroom, a disparity we term the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
